name: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA, a bile-acid medicine)
short: PSC trial, high dose: 2.1 times the risk of death, transplant or listing criteria; serious adverse events 63% vs 37% on placebo. Same dose, 56 with ulcerative colitis: more bowel dysplasia or cancer.
text: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) is a medicine used for chronic cholestatic liver diseases. In primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), a high dose was linked to serious harm. In a long-term randomised, double-blind trial in 150 adults with PSC, high-dose UDCA (28 to 30 mg/kg/day) was compared with placebo, with cirrhosis, varices, cholangiocarcinoma (bile-duct cancer), liver transplantation or death as the main outcomes; the trial was stopped after 6 years for futility. By the end, 30 patients on UDCA (39%) and 19 on placebo (26%) had reached one of these endpoints. After adjustment for baseline characteristics, the risk of a main endpoint was 2.3 times greater on UDCA (P < 0.01), and the risk of death, transplantation or reaching the minimal criteria for transplant listing was 2.1 times greater (P = 0.038). Serious adverse events were more common with UDCA (63% versus 37%, P < 0.01). In a follow-up of 56 people with ulcerative colitis and PSC from an earlier placebo-controlled trial of the same high dose, those given UDCA had a higher risk of colorectal neoplasia (dysplasia and cancer) (hazard ratio 4.44, 95% CI 1.30 to 20.10). A 2012 meta-analysis of 7 trials (553 patients) states that high-dose UDCA was associated with increased mortality in one of the large trials it included. On the other side, in a 5-year placebo-controlled trial of 17 to 23 mg/kg/day in 219 people with PSC, death or liver transplantation occurred in 7 of 97 (7.2%) on UDCA and 11 of 101 (10.9%) on placebo (P = .368). A follow-up of 98 of its patients who also had inflammatory bowel disease found dysplasia or cancer after 5 years in 13% of those originally given UDCA and 16% given placebo. A 2013 meta-analysis of 8 studies (763 people with PSC and inflammatory bowel disease) found no significant overall association between UDCA and colorectal neoplasia (odds ratio 0.81). A 2011 Cochrane review of 8 trials (592 patients, all at high risk of bias, doses from 10 to 30 mg/kg/day) described UDCA as safe and well tolerated in PSC. More generally, a 2003 systematic review found that UDCA caused diarrhoea in a small proportion of patients and that rare skin reactions were due to drug adjuvants rather than UDCA itself; decompensation of liver cirrhosis was reported in single cases of end-stage primary biliary cirrhosis, and recurrent upper right abdominal pain was observed incidentally. In pregnancy, in a placebo-controlled trial in 605 women with intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, given oral tablets, there were 2 serious adverse events with UDCA and 6 with placebo, none regarded as related to treatment; an individual-participant meta-analysis of 6974 women with this condition found stillbirth in 0.7% of fetuses with UDCA and 0.6% without (adjusted odds ratio 1.04, not significant). Interactions: the 2003 review reports that colestyramine, colestimide, colestipol, aluminium hydroxide and smectite impaired UDCA absorption, and that metabolic interactions were reported with ciclosporin, nitrendipine and dapsone, which are broken down by the liver enzyme cytochrome P450 3A.
